name: Ramp
text: Add a **large, high-contrast skip link** at the top of every page, visible by default. This lets keyboard users bypass repetitive navigation blocks in one click, solving a core keyboard-nav failure without hiding the tool from sighted users. The trade-off is slightly more screen space used, but the benefit for keyboard-only users outweighs the minimal layout impact.

name: Reader
text: A visible skip link risks pushing down other content, potentially burying crucial elements of the page. This could frustrate users who rely on keyboard navigation as they may find it harder to access important information. A better alternative is using a hidden skip link that becomes visible when focused, ensuring that screen-reader users can still navigate effectively without cluttering the visual layout for sighted users. Settling the argument would involve testing both options with keyboard users to gauge their preferences and usability.

name: Ramp
text:
We should add a **hidden skip link** that only appears when focused via keyboard, as this balances the need for easy keyboard navigation with the concern of not pushing down other content. This approach ensures that sighted users are not distracted by an always-visible skip link, while still providing keyboard users with a quick way to bypass repetitive navigation blocks. The trade-off is that users who rely on screen readers may not discover the skip link as easily, but this is mitigated by the link being announced by screen readers when keyboard focus is on it. By doing this, we prioritize a clean and uncluttered page layout while maintaining accessibility for keyboard users.

name: Reader
text: Hidden skip links confuse first-time keyboard users who don’t know they exist. A visible skip link risks pushing down content, but we can test placement—top-right, fixed position, or after the header—to minimize disruption. Settle this with user testing: measure time-to-task for keyboard users with both versions; the faster, clearer path wins.
